claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a multifactorial disease caused by irreversible progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a multifactorial disease caused by irreversible progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
evidence: This is a well-established characterization of Parkinson's disease supported by scientific consensus and citations in the introduction.

claim: Recent studies have reported the successful conversion of astrocytes into DANs by repressing polypyrimidine tract binding protein 1 (PTBP1), which led to the rescue of motor symptoms in a chemically-induced mouse model of PD.
source: Recent studies have reported the successful conversion of astrocytes into DANs by repressing polypyrimidine tract binding protein 1 (PTBP1), which led to the rescue of motor symptoms in a chemically-induced mouse model of PD.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Qian et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: Follow-up studies have questioned the validity of the astrocyte-to-DAN conversion model.
source: However, follow-up studies have questioned the validity of this astrocyte-to-DAN conversion model.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies (Chen et al., 2022; Hoang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021) mentioned in the introduction.

claim: PTBP1 downregulation in astrocytes had no effect in a chemically-induced PD mouse model.
source: While PTBP1 downregulation in astrocytes had no effect, PTBP1 downregulation in neurons of the striatum resulted in the expression of the DAN marker tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) in non-dividing neurons, which was associated with an increase in striatal dopamine concentrations and a rescue of forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including behavioral tests and histological analysis.

claim: PTBP1 downregulation in neurons of the striatum resulted in the expression of the DAN marker tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) in non-dividing neurons.
source: While PTBP1 downregulation in astrocytes had no effect, PTBP1 downregulation in neurons of the striatum resulted in the expression of the DAN marker tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) in non-dividing neurons, which was associated with an increase in striatal dopamine concentrations and a rescue of forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including immunohistochemistry and BrdU labeling experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: PTBP1 downregulation in neurons was associated with an increase in striatal dopamine concentrations.
source: While PTBP1 downregulation in astrocytes had no effect, PTBP1 downregulation in neurons of the striatum resulted in the expression of the DAN marker tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) in non-dividing neurons, which was associated with an increase in striatal dopamine concentrations and a rescue of forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations.
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: PTBP1 downregulation in neurons resulted in a rescue of forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations.
source: While PTBP1 downregulation in astrocytes had no effect, PTBP1 downregulation in neurons of the striatum resulted in the expression of the DAN marker tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) in non-dividing neurons, which was associated with an increase in striatal dopamine concentrations and a rescue of forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Most TH-positive cells co-expressed the dopaminergic marker DAT and the pan-neuronal marker NEUN.
source: Phenotypic analysis using multiplexed iterative immunofluorescence imaging further revealed that most of these TH-positive cells co-expressed the dopaminergic marker DAT and the pan-neuronal marker NEUN, with the majority of these triple-positive cells being classified as mature GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The majority of TH/DAT/NEUN triple-positive cells were classified as mature GABAergic neurons.
source: Phenotypic analysis using multiplexed iterative immunofluorescence imaging further revealed that most of these TH-positive cells co-expressed the dopaminergic marker DAT and the pan-neuronal marker NEUN, with the majority of these triple-positive cells being classified as mature GABAergic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data showing expression of GABAergic markers (CTIP2, PV, SST, CALB2) in Figure 4.

claim: PD is characterized by the progressive and irreversible loss of DANs in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), which leads to the disruption of the nigrostriatal pathway and depletion of striatal dopamine.
source: PD is a complex and multifactorial disorder, characterized by the progressive and irreversible loss of DANs in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), which leads to the disruption of the nigrostriatal pathway and depletion of striatal dopamine (Bloem et al., 2021; Gitler et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature (Bloem et al., 2021; Gitler et al., 2017; Moore et al., 2005).

claim: Current treatment strategies for PD do not focus on slowing down or halting disease progression, but rather aim to control symptoms and maintain the patients' quality of life.
source: In fact, current treatment strategies do not focus on slowing down or halting disease progression, but rather aim to control symptoms and maintain the patients' quality of life (Stoker and Barker, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stoker and Barker, 2020.

claim: Astrocytes are non-neuronal cells and thus not affected by neurodegeneration.
source: First, they are non-neuronal cells and thus not affected by neurodegeneration (Yu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2020.

claim: Astrocytes can acquire certain characteristics of neural stem cells, including multipotency, when activated.
source: Second, they can acquire certain characteristics of neural stem cells, including multipotency, when activated (Niu et al., 2013; Buffo et al., 2008; Robel et al., 2011; Shimada et al., 2012; Sirko et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Niu et al., 2013; Buffo et al., 2008; Robel et al., 2011; Shimada et al., 2012; Sirko et al., 2013).

claim: Astrocytes are highly proliferative in brain injuries such as neurodegeneration.
source: Finally, they are highly proliferative in brain injuries such as neurodegeneration (Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2021.

claim: Two recent studies have shown that repression of PTBP1 efficiently converts astrocytes into DANs in the SNc or striatum.
source: Moreover, two recent studies have shown that repression of the RNA-binding protein PTBP1, which mainly functions as a splicing regulator (Valcárcel and Gebauer, 1997), efficiently converts astrocytes into DANs in the SNc or striatum (Qian et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Qian et al., 2020 and Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: PTBP1 repression led to the restoration of the nigrostriatal pathway and striatal dopamine levels, as well as the rescue of motor deficits in a chemically-induced mouse model of PD.
source: Consequently, this led to the restoration of the nigrostriatal pathway and striatal dopamine levels, as well as the rescue of motor deficits in a chemically-induced mouse model of PD (Qian et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Qian et al., 2020 and Zhou et al., 2020.

claim: Stringent lineage-tracing strategies have revealed that neither quiescent nor reactive astrocytes convert to DANs upon PTBP1 depletion in the SNc or striatum.
source: However, since the publication of these two studies in 2020, stringent lineage-tracing strategies have revealed that neither quiescent nor reactive astrocytes convert to DANs upon PTBP1 depletion in the SNc or striatum (Chen et al., 2022; Hoang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021), fueling widespread debate about the origin of these de novo generated cells and their ability to alleviate motor deficits in PD mice (Arenas, 2020; Jiang et al., 2021; Qian et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2022; Hoang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Adenine base editors (ABEs) enable gene editing independent of DNA double-strand break formation.
source: In this study, we employed adenine base editors (ABEs), which enable gene editing independent of DNA double-strand break formation (Gaudelli et al., 2017) and thus without the risk of inducing chromosomal rearrangements, translocations, or large deletions (Adikusuma et al., 2018; Kosicki et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2017), to install a loss-of-function splice mutation in the Ptbp1 gene in astrocytes or neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gaudelli et al., 2017.

claim: ABEs do not carry the risk of inducing chromosomal rearrangements, translocations, or large deletions.
source: In this study, we employed adenine base editors (ABEs), which enable gene editing independent of DNA double-strand break formation (Gaudelli et al., 2017) and thus without the risk of inducing chromosomal rearrangements, translocations, or large deletions (Adikusuma et al., 2018; Kosicki et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2017), to install a loss-of-function splice mutation in the Ptbp1 gene in astrocytes or neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Adikusuma et al., 2018; Kosicki et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2017.

claim: Downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 in the SNc and striatum improves forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations in a chemically-induced PD mouse model.
source: Using a chemically-induced PD mouse model, we show that downregulation of neuronal rather than astroglial PTBP1 in the SNc and striatum improves forelimb akinesia and spontaneous rotations.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 induced expression of TH in non-dividing neurons of the striatum.
source: Histological analysis revealed that downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 induced expression of TH, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of dopamine and other catecholamines and thus a characteristic marker of DANs, in non-dividing neurons of the striatum.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and BrdU labeling data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: TH is the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of dopamine and other catecholamines.
source: Histological analysis revealed that downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 induced expression of TH, which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the biosynthesis of dopamine and other catecholamines and thus a characteristic marker of DANs, in non-dividing neurons of the striatum.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about TH function.

claim: Lack or dysfunction of TH results in dopamine deficiency and parkinsonism.
source: Since lack or dysfunction of TH results in dopamine deficiency and parkinsonism, induction of TH expression in striatal neurons may explain the observed rescue of PD phenotypes in mice and provide therapeutic benefits for PD patients.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of TH in dopamine synthesis and Parkinson's disease.

claim: Base editors can be applied to precisely disrupt canonical splice sites and permanently eliminate gene function in vivo.
source: BEs can thus be applied to precisely disrupt canonical splice sites and permanently eliminate gene function in vivo (Kluesner et al., 2021; Musunuru et al., 2021; Rothgangl et al., 2021; Winter et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kluesner et al., 2021; Musunuru et al., 2021; Rothgangl et al., 2021; Winter et al., 2019.

claim: Base editing activity was higher at splice donor sites, with the highest editing rates at the exon-intron junctions of exon 3 (92.9 ± 1.0% for SpG-ABE8e) and 7 (85.0 ± 7.2% for SpCas-ABE8e).
source: In line with previous reports (Kluesner et al., 2021), base editing activity was higher at splice donor sites, with the highest editing rates at the exon-intron junctions of exon 3 (92.9 ± 1.0% for SpG-ABE8e) and 7 (85.0 ± 7.2% for SpCas-ABE8e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Average editing rates of 77% (sgRNA-ex3) and 73% (sgRNA-ex7) on genomic DNA resulted in approximately 70% and 50% reduction of Ptbp1 transcripts in Hepa cells.
source: Average editing rates of 77% (sgRNA-ex3) and 73% (sgRNA-ex7) on genomic DNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) resulted in approximately 70% (p<0.0004) and 50% reduction of Ptbp1 transcripts (p<0.0064) in Hepa cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), leading to a substantial reduction in PTBP1 protein levels and a significant increase in the transcription of exons known to be repressed by PTBP1 (Han et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Figure 1—figure supplement 2; for sgRNA-ex3: Ptbp2, p<0.0014; Ptbp3, p<0.0051; Kcnq2, p<0.0317; for sgRNA-ex7, Ptbp2, p<0.0477; Ptbp3, p<0.0055; Kcnq2, p<0.0160).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Editing of the canonical splice donor at exon 3 generated alternative Ptbp1 splice sites in all three cell lines.
source: Notably, editing of the canonical splice donor at exon 3 generated alternative Ptbp1 splice sites in all three cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which, however, did not result in functional PTBP1 protein (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Western blot data in Figure 1C.

claim: Alternative Ptbp1 splice sites generated by editing did not result in functional PTBP1 protein.
source: Notably, editing of the canonical splice donor at exon 3 generated alternative Ptbp1 splice sites in all three cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), which, however, did not result in functional PTBP1 protein (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced PTBP1 protein levels in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 6-OHDA induced a severe unilateral lesion in the nigrostriatal pathway, characterized by an average 99% reduction in the number of TH+ DANs in the SNc ipsilateral to the injection site.
source: As expected, 6-OHDA induced a severe unilateral lesion in the nigrostriatal pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), characterized by an average 99% reduction in the number of TH+ DANs in the SNc ipsilateral to the injection site (intact hemisphere: 10547 ± 2313 TH+ cells; lesioned hemisphere: 114 ± 83 TH+ cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and an average 92% decrease in fluorescence signal corresponding to striatal DA fibers (dorsal, p<0.0001; ventral, p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 6-OHDA induced an average 92% decrease in fluorescence signal corresponding to striatal DA fibers.
source: As expected, 6-OHDA induced a severe unilateral lesion in the nigrostriatal pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), characterized by an average 99% reduction in the number of TH+ DANs in the SNc ipsilateral to the injection site (intact hemisphere: 10547 ± 2313 TH+ cells; lesioned hemisphere: 114 ± 83 TH+ cells; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and an average 92% decrease in fluorescence signal corresponding to striatal DA fibers (dorsal, p<0.0001; ventral, p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A sharp increase in activated astrocytes was observed following 6-OHDA lesion, as indicated by the upregulation of GFAP.
source: In line with previous reports (Chen et al., 2022), we also observed a sharp increase in activated astrocytes, as indicated by the upregulation of the intermediate filament protein GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Chen et al., 2022.

claim: Ipsilateral rotations and contralateral forelimb akinesia were significantly increased following 6-OHDA lesion.
source: Finally, we analyzed perturbations in spontaneous motor activities following the 6-OHDA lesion (Boix et al., 2015; Glajch et al., 2012; Iancu et al., 2005) and found that ipsilateral rotations (p=0.0012) and contralateral forelimb akinesia (P<0.0001) were significantly increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to Boix et al., 2015; Glajch et al., 2012; Iancu et al., 2005.

claim: Animals treated with AAV-hsyn to downregulate PTBP1 in neurons showed a restoration of approximately 10% of TH+ cells compared to the intact hemisphere.
source: When we next assessed animals treated with AAV-hsyn to downregulate PTBP1 in neurons, we observed a restoration of approximately 10% of TH+ cells compared to the intact hemisphere (intact hemisphere: 7613 ± 1386 TH+ cells; lesioned hemisphere: 721 ± 144 TH+ cells; Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claim: Animals treated with AAV-GFAP to downregulate PTBP1 in astrocytes did not observe TH+ cells above control levels.
source: In contrast, when we analyzed animals treated with AAV-GFAP to downregulate PTBP1 in astrocytes, we did not observe TH+ cells above control levels (intact hemisphere: 9209 ± 1199 TH+ cells; lesioned hemisphere: 158 ± 78 TH+ cells; Figure 2C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: TH+ cells generated in the SNc upon neuronal PTBP1 downregulation did not form striatal projections.
source: However, despite the presence of TH + cells in the SNc of AAV-hsyn-treated animals, we did not detect an increase in fluorescence signal corresponding to DA fibers in the striatum (ventral: AAV-GFAP, p=0.7935; AAV-hsyn, p=0.6998; dorsal: AAV-GFAP, p=0.7352; AAV-hsyn, p=0.4906), suggesting that TH+ cells generated in the SNc upon neuronal PTBP1 downregulation did not form striatal projections (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis of striatal DA fibers shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: No differences in fluorescence intensity were detected between groups when analyzing projections of DANs in the mfb.
source: Further supporting this observation, we did not detect differences in fluorescence intensity between groups when analyzing projections of DANs in the mfb (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; AAV-GFAP, p=0.3796; AAV-hsyn, p=0.2996).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site was 14.7 ± 3.9% for AAV-GFAP and 15.5 ± 8.5% for AAV-hsyn in SNc tissues.
source: Notably, base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site (AAV-ctrl, 0.04 ± 0.03%, AAV-GFAP, 14.7 ± 3.9%; AAV-hsyn, 15.5 ± 8.5%) as well as a reduction of Ptbp1 transcript (AAV-GFAP, 23.7 ± 12.7%, p=0.0383; AAV-hsyn, 24.8 ± 18.7%, p=0.0354) and PTBP1 protein levels (AAV-GFAP, 10.8 ± 6.3%; AAV-hsyn, 13.8 ± 10.1%) could be confirmed in SNc tissues at experimental endpoints (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Reduction of Ptbp1 transcript was 23.7 ± 12.7% for AAV-GFAP and 24.8 ± 18.7% for AAV-hsyn in SNc tissues.
source: Notably, base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site (AAV-ctrl, 0.04 ± 0.03%, AAV-GFAP, 14.7 ± 3.9%; AAV-hsyn, 15.5 ± 8.5%) as well as a reduction of Ptbp1 transcript (AAV-GFAP, 23.7 ± 12.7%, p=0.0383; AAV-hsyn, 24.8 ± 18.7%, p=0.0354) and PTBP1 protein levels (AAV-GFAP, 10.8 ± 6.3%; AAV-hsyn, 13.8 ± 10.1%) could be confirmed in SNc tissues at experimental endpoints (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: 106±38 TH+ cells were found across 3 sections in the striatum of mice treated with AAV-hsyn.
source: When we quantified TH+ cells in brain sections of the striatum, we found 106±38 TH+ cells across 3 sections (estimated as 2646±952 cells in the entire striatum) in mice treated with AAV-hsyn compared to no TH+ cells in the lesioned hemisphere of animals treated with AAV-ctrl (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site was 23.0 ± 6.6% in striatum tissues of AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice.
source: Analysis of striatum tissues isolated from AAV-ctrl- and AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice revealed base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site (AAV-ctrl, 0.4 ± 0.1%; AAV-hsyn, 23.0 ± 6.6%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and downregulation of Ptbp1 transcript (AAV-hsyn, 30.8 ± 14.6%, P=0.0681) and PTBP1 protein levels (AAV-hsyn, 22.1 ± 6.4%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Downregulation of Ptbp1 transcript was 30.8 ± 14.6% in striatum tissues of AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice.
source: Analysis of striatum tissues isolated from AAV-ctrl- and AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice revealed base editing at the Ptbp1 splice site (AAV-ctrl, 0.4 ± 0.1%; AAV-hsyn, 23.0 ± 6.6%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and downregulation of Ptbp1 transcript (AAV-hsyn, 30.8 ± 14.6%, P=0.0681) and PTBP1 protein levels (AAV-hsyn, 22.1 ± 6.4%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Virtually all TH+ cells in the intact SNc were co-stained for NEUN (99.0 ± 0.1%).
source: As expected, virtually all TH+ cells in the intact SNc were co-stained for NEUN (99.0 ± 0.1%; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The majority of TH+ cells in the lesioned SNc (92.0 ± 6.2%) and striatum (77.5 ± 11.8%) of AAV-hsyn-treated animals were labeled by NEUN.
source: Likewise, the majority of TH+ cells in the lesioned SNc (hsyn: 92.0 ± 6.2%; Figure 3B) and striatum of AAV-hsyn-treated animals (77.5 ± 11.8%; Figure 3C) were also labeled by NEUN, further corroborating a neuronal origin of these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: A significant reduction in the surface area and Feret's diameter was observed between TH/NEUN double-positive cells in the lesioned striatum compared to endogenous DANs in the intact SNc.
source: Moreover, we observed a significant reduction in the surface area (p<0.0001) and Feret's diameter (p<0.0001) between TH/NEUN double-positive cells in the lesioned striatum compared to endogenous DANs in the intact SNc, or TH/NEUN double-positive cell bodies in the lesioned SNc of AAV-hsyn-treated mice (Figure 3D; surface area, p<0.001; Feret's diameter, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Injection of AAV-hsyn into the visual cortex did not lead to TH expression in local neurons.
source: In line with previous work (Qian et al., 2020), injection of AAV-hsyn into the visual cortex did not lead to TH expression in local neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 5; n=174 Cas9/NEUN double-positive cells), suggesting that the local microenvironment indeed plays a contributing role in inducing TH expression in the targeted neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and a citation to Qian et al., 2020.

claim: Microscopic analysis of 163 TH/NEUN double-positive cells revealed no co-labeling with BrdU.
source: Microscopic analysis of 163 TH/NEUN double-positive cells revealed no co-labeling with BrdU (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), indicating that TH+ cells were not generated de novo and rather originated from non-proliferating mature neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: TH+ cells were not generated de novo and rather originated from non-proliferating mature neurons.
source: Microscopic analysis of 163 TH/NEUN double-positive cells revealed no co-labeling with BrdU (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), indicating that TH+ cells were not generated de novo and rather originated from non-proliferating mature neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of BrdU labeling in TH/NEUN double-positive cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The majority of TH+ cells also expressed the marker DAT (75.2 ± 5.6%).
source: The majority of TH+ cells also expressed the marker DAT (75.2 ± 5.6%; Figure 4A and B), further corroborating the DA identity of these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Only a small fraction of TH/DAT double-positive cells were labeled for markers of neural progenitors (SOX2, 9.1 ± 2.4%; NESTIN, 2.1 ± 0.5%; DCX, 2.6 ± 0.8%).
source: Moreover, supporting the results of our BrdU-labeling experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 6), only a small fraction of TH/DAT double-positive cells were labeled for markers of neural progenitors (SOX2, 9.1 ± 2.4%; NESTIN, 2.1 ± 0.5%; DCX, 2.6 ± 0.8%; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Most TH/DAT-labeled cells expressed the adult pan-neuronal marker NEUN (86.2 ± 3.7%).
source: Instead, most TH/DAT-labeled cells expressed the adult pan-neuronal marker NEUN (86.2 ± 3.7%; Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Of the TH/DAT/NEUN-positive population, 49.8 ± 12.9% were additionally labeled with CTIP2, a marker for GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs).
source: Of this TH/DAT/NEUN-positive population, 49.8 ± 12.9% were additionally labeled with CTIP2 (Figure 4A and B), a marker for GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs), and 46.4 ± 10.4% expressed markers for various GABAergic interneurons (PV, 3.2 ± 1.9%; SST, 3.5 ± 1.2%; CALB2, 39.7 ± 11.0%; Figure 4A and B), indicating that expression of DA markers may be achieved in various subtypes of GABAergic neurons upon PTBP1 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: 46.4 ± 10.4% of TH/DAT/NEUN-positive cells expressed markers for various GABAergic interneurons (PV, 3.2 ± 1.9%; SST, 3.5 ± 1.2%; CALB2, 39.7 ± 11.0%).
source: Of this TH/DAT/NEUN-positive population, 49.8 ± 12.9% were additionally labeled with CTIP2 (Figure 4A and B), a marker for GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs), and 46.4 ± 10.4% expressed markers for various GABAergic interneurons (PV, 3.2 ± 1.9%; SST, 3.5 ± 1.2%; CALB2, 39.7 ± 11.0%; Figure 4A and B), indicating that expression of DA markers may be achieved in various subtypes of GABAergic neurons upon PTBP1 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by 4i imaging data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Expression of DA markers may be achieved in various subtypes of GABAergic neurons upon PTBP1 downregulation.
source: Of this TH/DAT/NEUN-positive population, 49.8 ± 12.9% were additionally labeled with CTIP2 (Figure 4A and B), a marker for GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs), and 46.4 ± 10.4% expressed markers for various GABAergic interneurons (PV, 3.2 ± 1.9%; SST, 3.5 ± 1.2%; CALB2, 39.7 ± 11.0%; Figure 4A and B), indicating that expression of DA markers may be achieved in various subtypes of GABAergic neurons upon PTBP1 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the 4i imaging data showing expression of GABAergic markers in TH/DAT/NEUN-positive cells in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Drug-free motor dysfunctions were significantly alleviated in animals treated with AAV-hsyn in the SNc.
source: We found that drug-free motor dysfunctions were significantly alleviated in animals treated with AAV-hsyn (stepping test, p<0.0001; cylinder test, p<0.0001), but not with AAV-GFAP (stepping test, p=0.8608; cylinder test, p=0.0504), in the SNc when using an AAV dose of 2×108 vg per animal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Drug-free motor dysfunctions were not significantly alleviated in animals treated with AAV-GFAP in the SNc.
source: We found that drug-free motor dysfunctions were significantly alleviated in animals treated with AAV-hsyn (stepping test, p<0.0001; cylinder test, p<0.0001), but not with AAV-GFAP (stepping test, p=0.8608; cylinder test, p=0.0504), in the SNc when using an AAV dose of 2×108 vg per animal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PTBP1 targeting in striatal neurons restored the asymmetry of spontaneous behaviors.
source: Likewise, PTBP1 targeting in striatal neurons restored the asymmetry of spontaneous behaviors (AAV-hsyn: stepping test, p<0.0001; cylinder test, p<0.0001; AAV-ctrl: stepping test, p=0.2667; cylinder test, p=0.1870; Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: No recovery of contralateral rotations was detected in treated animals after systemic administration of amphetamine.
source: However, we did not detect recovery of contralateral rotations in treated animals after systemic administration of amphetamine (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), which leads to an enhanced imbalance of extracellular dopamine concentrations between the denervated and intact striatum (Freyberg et al., 2016; Karam et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No recovery of ipsilateral rotations was observed in any treatment group after systemic administration of apomorphine.
source: Likewise, after systemic administration of apomorphine, which acts as a dopamine receptor agonist and stimulates hypersensitive dopamine receptors in the lesioned hemisphere (Arroyo-García et al., 2018; da Conceição et al., 2010; Iancu et al., 2005), we did not observe a recovery of ipsilateral rotations in any treatment group (Figure 5D; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Delivery of dual AAV vectors to the SNc resulted in the formation of TH-expressing cells and the rescue of spontaneous behaviors when a neuronal promoter was used to drive ABE expression.
source: Delivery of dual AAV vectors to the SNc resulted in the formation of TH-expressing cells and the rescue of spontaneous behaviors when a neuronal promoter was used to drive ABE expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: No DA projections to the striatum were detected following neuronal PTBP1 downregulation in the SNc.
source: However, no DA projections to the striatum were detected, supporting recent findings that suggest a functional role of PTBP1 in promoting axon regeneration of adult sensory neurons (Alber et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2E and F and a citation to Alber et al., 2023.

claim: Reconstitution of the nigrostriatal pathway is unlikely the mechanism underlying the observed phenotypic rescue.
source: Reconstitution of the nigrostriatal pathway, which connects the SNc with the dorsal striatum (Kalia and Lang, 2015), is therefore unlikely the mechanism underlying the observed phenotypic rescue.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of DA projections to the striatum despite behavioral improvements.

claim: The downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 in the striatum of 6-OHDA-lesioned mice led to the formation of TH+ cells and a rescue of spontaneous behaviors.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the downregulation of neuronal PTBP1 in the striatum of 6-OHDA-lesioned mice also led to the formation of TH+ cells and a rescue of spontaneous behaviors.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The study contributes to evidence indicating that downregulation of astroglial PTBP1 does not induce astrocyte conversion into DANs.
source: Our study contributes to this recently growing body of evidence, indicating that downregulation of astroglial PTBP1 does not induce astrocyte conversion into DANs, and that neurons are the origin of the observed TH+ cells (Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and citations to Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023.

claim: Neurons are the origin of the observed TH+ cells.
source: Our study contributes to this recently growing body of evidence, indicating that downregulation of astroglial PTBP1 does not induce astrocyte conversion into DANs, and that neurons are the origin of the observed TH+ cells (Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing NEUN co-labeling in TH+ cells and citations to Chen et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2023.

claim: 4i and BrdU experiments revealed that TH expression in the striatum was induced in mature neurons, either expressing markers of GABAergic MSNs or interneurons.
source: Our 4i and BrdU experiments furthermore revealed that TH expression in the striatum was induced in mature neurons, either expressing markers of GABAergic MSNs or interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The interplay between microRNAs (miRNAs) and the RNA processing proteins PTBP1 and nPTBP is crucial during neuronal differentiation and maturation.
source: Previous research has demonstrated that the interplay between microRNAs (miRNAs) and the RNA processing proteins PTBP1 and its homology nPTBP (PTBP2) is crucial during neuronal differentiation and maturation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Boutz et al., 2007; Makeyev et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boutz et al., 2007; Makeyev et al., 2007; Zheng et al., 2012.

claim: The activation of the PTBP1/nPTBP regulatory loops is essential for driving reprogramming toward the neuronal lineage and subsequent neuronal maturation.
source: Thus, the activation of the PTBP1/nPTBP regulatory loops is essential for driving reprogramming toward the neuronal lineage and subsequent neuronal maturation (Xue et al., 2016; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xue et al., 2016; Xue et al., 2013.

claim: PTBP1 is sufficiently expressed and plays a functional role in mature neurons.
source: While this classical model of PTBP1 down-regulation and neuronal differentiation implies negligible expression or importance of PTBP1 in mature neurons, our results indicate that PTBP1 is sufficiently expressed and plays a functional role in mature neurons, with the installation of a loss-of-function mutation resulting in a detectable reduction in relative protein amounts (Figure 2—figure supplement 5; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and behavioral improvements in a PD mouse model (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data showing PTBP1 expression in mature neurons and behavioral improvements upon PTBP1 downregulation.

claim: A recent study demonstrated PTBP1 expression in axons of sensory and motor neurons as well as a functional role in sensation, injury response, and axonal regeneration.
source: Supporting these findings, a recent study demonstrated PTBP1 expression in axons of sensory and motor neurons as well as a functional role in sensation, injury response, and axonal regeneration (Alber et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alber et al., 2023.

claim: Both MSNs and interneurons receive DA inputs from the SNc.
source: Since both MSNs and interneurons receive DA inputs from the SNc, their activity, and excitability are strongly hampered when striatal dopamine is absent (Bamford et al., 2018; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bamford et al., 2018; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Kreitzer and Malenka, 2008.

claim: PTBP1 downregulation by adenine base editing and subsequent TH expression might have enabled local dopamine synthesis in the dorsal striatum.
source: It, therefore, seems feasible that PTBP1 downregulation by adenine base editing and subsequent TH expression might have enabled local dopamine synthesis in the dorsal striatum, which may have been sufficient to partly restore the function of these cell populations and compensate for the depletion of DA inputs from the SNc.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on inference from the observed TH expression and dopamine increase.

claim: Depletion of GPR6 in D2-MSNs reduced intracellular cAMP concentrations, leading to increased striatal dopamine and decreased involuntary movements following apomorphine treatment in 6-OHDA-lesioned PD mice.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, a recent study has shown that depletion of the orphan G-protein coupled receptor 6 (GPR6) in D2-MSNs reduced intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) concentrations, leading to increased striatal dopamine and decreased involuntary movements following apomorphine treatment in 6-OHDA-lesioned PD mice (Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2021.

claim: A 2.5-fold increase in striatal dopamine was observed in AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice using HPLC.
source: When we quantified dopamine levels in the striatum of AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice using HPLC, we observed a 2.5-fold increase in striatal dopamine, suggesting that induction of TH expression in striatal neurons might establish a basal tone of extracellular dopamine despite the absence of striatal DA projections, akin to pharmacological replenishment in PD patients (Poewe et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Induction of TH expression in striatal neurons might establish a basal tone of extracellular dopamine despite the absence of striatal DA projections.
source: When we quantified dopamine levels in the striatum of AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice using HPLC, we observed a 2.5-fold increase in striatal dopamine, suggesting that induction of TH expression in striatal neurons might establish a basal tone of extracellular dopamine despite the absence of striatal DA projections, akin to pharmacological replenishment in PD patients (Poewe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative claim inferred from the observed dopamine increase and behavioral improvements.

claim: Even a modest increase in striatal dopamine is sufficient to rescue spontaneous motor behaviors in PD mice.
source: While the increase in dopamine levels was modest compared to 6-OHDA-lesioned rats treated with the dopamine precursor L-DOPA, which exhibited an increase in extracellular dopamine concentrations from ~0.04 fmol/µL to ~9–10 fmol/µL (Lindgren et al., 2010), our results indicate that even a modest increase in striatal dopamine is sufficient to rescue spontaneous motor behaviors in PD mice.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the behavioral improvements observed despite modest dopamine increases.

claim: Multiple unconditioned DA-dependent motor tasks can be sustained through a diffuse basal tone of extracellular dopamine in the striatum.
source: This finding aligns with recent work showing that multiple unconditioned DA-dependent motor tasks can be sustained through a diffuse basal tone of extracellular dopamine in the striatum (Delignat-Lavaud et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Delignat-Lavaud et al., 2023.

claim: Basal dopamine levels were insufficient to improve amphetamine-induced behaviors in AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice.
source: Conversely, basal dopamine levels were insufficient to improve amphetamine-induced behaviors in AAV-hsyn-treated PD mice in this study, potentially due to the lack of striatal projections from the SNc and/or insufficient availability of intracellular dopamine in striatal neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The detected dopamine levels in striatal tissues were not sufficient to reverse the hypersensitivity of D1 and D2 receptors to the dopamine agonist apomorphine.
source: Likewise, the detected dopamine levels in striatal tissues were not sufficient to reverse the hypersensitivity of D1 and D2 receptors to the dopamine agonist apomorphine.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Base-edited animals showed an approximately 2.5-fold increase in the concentration of striatal dopamine (AAV-hsyn: 4.4 ± 2.6 nmol/g protein; AAV-ctrl: 1.7 ± 0.7 nmol/g protein; p=0.0159).
source: Importantly, base-edited animals showed an approximately 2.5-fold increase in the concentration of striatal dopamine (AAV-hsyn: 4.4 ± 2.6 nmol/g protein; AAV-ctrl: 1.7 ± 0.7 nmol/g protein; p=0.0159) and the dopamine metabolite 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid (DOPAC; AAV-hsyn: 8.2 ± 3.9 nmol/g protein; AAV-ctrl: 3.1 ± 1.8 nmol/g protein; p=0.0449) in the lesioned hemisphere (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Base-edited animals showed an increase in the dopamine metabolite DOPAC (AAV-hsyn: 8.2 ± 3.9 nmol/g protein; AAV-ctrl: 3.1 ± 1.8 nmol/g protein; p=0.0449) in the lesioned hemisphere.
source: Importantly, base-edited animals showed an approximately 2.5-fold increase in the concentration of striatal dopamine (AAV-hsyn: 4.4 ± 2.6 nmol/g protein; AAV-ctrl: 1.7 ± 0.7 nmol/g protein; p=0.0159) and the dopamine metabolite 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid (DOPAC; AAV-hsyn: 8.2 ± 3.9 nmol/g protein; AAV-ctrl: 3.1 ± 1.8 nmol/g protein; p=0.0449) in the lesioned hemisphere (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: Editing rates were lower in N2a (64 ± 7.9%) and C8-D1A (62.7 ± 15.1%) cell lines compared to Hepa cells (92.9 ± 1.0%).
source: Compared to Hepa cells (92.9 ± 1.0%; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), editing rates were lower in both cell lines (N2a: 64 ± 7.9%; C8-D1A: 62.7 ± 15.1%; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A substantial reduction of Ptbp1 mRNA was detected in N2a (p<0.0073) and C8-D1A (P<0.0275) cells.
source: Nevertheless, we again detected a substantial reduction of Ptbp1 mRNA (N2a, p<0.0073; C8-D1A, P<0.0275) and PTBP1 protein levels (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: One off-target site was identified in the myopalladin (Mypn) gene.
source: One off-target site was identified in the myopalladin (Mypn) gene, which encodes for a muscle-specific protein and plays a critical role in regulating the structure and growth of skeletal and cardiac muscle (Filomena et al., 2021; Filomena et al., 2020), and another site was detected in the intronic region of the ankyrin-1 (Ank1) gene, which encodes for an adaptor protein linking membrane proteins to the underlying cytoskeleton (Cunha and Mohler, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by GUIDE-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Another off-target site was detected in the intronic region of the ankyrin-1 (Ank1) gene.
source: One off-target site was identified in the myopalladin (Mypn) gene, which encodes for a muscle-specific protein and plays a critical role in regulating the structure and growth of skeletal and cardiac muscle (Filomena et al., 2021; Filomena et al., 2020), and another site was detected in the intronic region of the ankyrin-1 (Ank1) gene, which encodes for an adaptor protein linking membrane proteins to the underlying cytoskeleton (Cunha and Mohler, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by GUIDE-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Base editing rates at both off-target sites were substantially lower (Mypn, 5.4 ± 1.7%; Ank1, 5.8±1.9%) than at the Ptbp1 site in AAV-hsyn-treated mice (23.0 ± 6.6%).
source: Importantly, base editing rates at both sites were substantially lower (Mypn, 5.4 ± 1.7%; Ank1, 5.8±1.9%; Figure 3—figure supplement 3) than at the Ptbp1 site in AAV-hsyn-treated mice (23.0 ± 6.6%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and no reduction in transcript levels of the respective genes was observed (Mypn, P=0.4528; Ank1, P=0.5547; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: No reduction in transcript levels of Mypn and Ank1 was observed (Mypn, P=0.4528; Ank1, P=0.5547).
source: Importantly, base editing rates at both sites were substantially lower (Mypn, 5.4 ± 1.7%; Ank1, 5.8±1.9%; Figure 3—figure supplement 3) than at the Ptbp1 site in AAV-hsyn-treated mice (23.0 ± 6.6%; Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and no reduction in transcript levels of the respective genes was observed (Mypn, P=0.4528; Ank1, P=0.5547; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The induction of TH expression upon adenine base editing with sgRNA-ex3 is likely a direct consequence of PTBP1 downregulation.
source: Thus, the induction of TH expression upon adenine base editing with sgRNA-ex3 is likely a direct consequence of PTBP1 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of significant off-target effects and the correlation between PTBP1 downregulation and TH expression.
